scenes.headline: How a code corpus is built, and counted without downloading
scenes.sub: UltraData-Code: 1.2 TB of parquet, measured through APIs on 1.3 GB of disk.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Petunia! UltraData-Code is a tiered code corpus in eleven languages. Here's how it's built, and how to count it without downloading it.

scenes.label: The idea
scenes.text: Code is sifted in tiers: filter GitHub, score every file for role, relevance and quality, then turn the survivors into exercises.

scenes.title: Four tiers, from GitHub to exercises

steps.say: It starts from public GitHub. L1 screens and cleans files, and groups near-duplicates, keeping the top-ranked half of each group.
L2 selects. A role model labels each file, like algorithm, tool or config, then a relevance score and a quality gate decide what stays.
L3 turns selected code into exercises: a task, an analysis, a solution and tests, each stored in its own column.

steps.note: the label and scores ship inside every row
steps.say: And every L2 row carries its own label and scores, so anyone can audit the selection.

items.text: Exact rows from the size endpoint
items.say: Row counts are exact, and free, from the Hub's size endpoint.
The statistics endpoint gives each column's mean length.
Tokenizing five hundred sampled rows per split gives characters per token.
The check: the method predicts the whole corpus's in-memory size to within zero point zero seven percent.

scenes.title: Relevance floor, by language
scenes.note: the lowest surviving score in each split is the cut
scenes.say: The thresholds were never published, but the lowest surviving score is the cut. The strictest languages need zero point eight five. Python's floor is zero.

scenes.label: tokens in L3's content column, the one the default config loads
scenes.note: the card's ~150B is the full_content column
scenes.say: One catch: the card's hundred and fifty billion counts L3's full-content column. The default content column holds fifty-two point four billion, about a third.

scenes.text: Ship the scores inside the rows, and anyone can read a corpus's thresholds straight off the data.

recap: L0 to L3: archive, filter, select, synthesize
Exact rows, sampled lengths, a byte cross-check
Scores in every row make the cut auditable
scenes.say: To recap: four tiers, a count you can check, and thresholds that sit in the data.
